extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Locke; advanced undergraduates studying metaphysics/personal identity
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic criteria concerning relations (relation, cause/effect, time/place) and the metaphysics of identity and personal identity, focusing on what grounds sameness over time. Useful for evaluating arguments about identity, persistence, and personhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation is the considering of one thing with another which is extrinsical to it; a way of comparing or considering two things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a single man may simultaneously bear many relations (father, brother, son, general, judge, friend, enemy, etc.). Relation arises from comparison and sometimes the relation itself is given a name. Related ideas are often simple or composed of simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relations often clearer than ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: THE IDEAS, THEN, OF RELATIONS, ARE CAPABLE AT LEAST OF BEING MORE PERFECT AND DISTINCT IN OUR MINDS THAN THOSE OF SUBSTANCES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the notion of FATHER or BROTHER is clearer than that of MAN; PATERNITY is easier to conceive than HUMANITY. Knowing one action or simple idea is often sufficient to grasp a relation, whereas a substantial being requires an accurate collection of sundry ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All ideas of relation ultimately end in the simple ideas of sensation or reflection, which are the materials of all our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even remote relations (e.g., cause and effect) are derived from simple ideas. Argument: show major relations trace back to sensation/reflection to demonstrate their ultimate origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms that lead the mind beyond the subject denominated are relative
rubrics_metrics.description: All words that necessarily lead the mind to any other ideas than those supposed really to exist in the thing are relative words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: absolute terms (MAN, BLACK, MERRY) do not intimate anything beyond the thing itself; relative terms (FATHER, BROTHER, KING, BLACKER, MERRIER) imply something exterior to the thing named.

rubrics_metrics.name: All relatives are made up of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of relations, however refined or remote, are composed only of simple ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed by showing main relations (e.g., cause/effect) reduce to simple ideas; use examples and reductive analysis to establish composition from simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and Effect: definition and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: THAT WHICH PRODUCES ANY SIMPLE OR COMPLEX IDEA is denoted by the general name CAUSE, and THAT WHICH IS PRODUCED, EFFECT. The notion arises from observing that some qualities or substances begin to exist through the operation of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heat producing fluidity in wax; fire turning wood into ashes. To have the idea of cause and effect it suffices to consider a simple idea or substance as beginning to exist by the operation of some other, without knowing the manner of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of origination: creation, generation, making, alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish origins: CREATION (thing wholly new, no part existed before), GENERATION (assembled from pre-existing particles by natural internal principle), MAKING (extrinsic cause and sensible composition—artificial things), ALTERATION (production of a simple idea not previously in the subject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a new particle of matter = creation; a man, egg, rose = generation; a picture = making; change of a sensible quality = alteration. Use these categories to classify causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations of time are relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Denominations received from time (how long, when) are relations indicating duration or distance within a larger time measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Queen Elizabeth lived sixty-nine years' expresses relation of that duration to the solar year; historical dates (e.g., 1066) express distance from a chosen epoch. Treat temporal expressions as comparative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some temporal terms thought positive are relative (young/old)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like YOUNG and OLD are relative, indicating comparison to a standard idea of ordinary duration for that kind of thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man is young at twenty, very young at seven; a horse is old at twenty, a dog at seven. Standards differ by species; celestial bodies are not called old because no standard lifetime is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations of place and extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Denominations concerning place and bulk (above, below, a mile distant; GREAT, LITTLE) are relational—they compare against standard ideas of size or position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'great apple' means bigger than ordinary apples; 'a great horse to a Welchman is little to a Fleming'—standards vary by customary experience and breed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute terms often stand for relations (e.g., weak/strong, necessary/stores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many words that appear absolute (weak, strong, necessary) function as relative terms, signifying disproportion or relation to some standard or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'weak man' = not as strong as usual men; 'creatures are weak' = relative to the power of God; 'necessary stores' = relative to accomplishing the intended voyage or future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity consists in sameness at a determined time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity arises when considering anything as existing at a determined time and place and comparing it with itself at another time; identity holds when its attributed ideas do not vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this follows that one thing cannot have two beginnings of existence, nor two things one beginning, since two things of the same kind cannot be in the same place at the same time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of Substances: God, finite intelligences, bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Three sorts of substances with identity rules: (1) GOD—eternal/unalterable so identity is unquestioned; (2) FINITE SPIRITS—identity determined by their determinated time/place of beginning; (3) BODIES—identity of a particle persists if no addition/subtraction of matter is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different identity criteria depending on the sort of substance under consideration; note contradictions if two bodies could occupy same place/time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of modes and relations vs. succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes/relations (e.g., motion, thought) that exist only in succession lack identity across times in the way permanent substances do, because they perish the moment they begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MOTION and THOUGHT are continued trains of succession; when considered at different times they cannot be the same in the sense used for permanent substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principium individuationis: existence itself individuates
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence (being at a particular time and place) is the principle that individuates a being and determines its identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an atom existing at an instant is the same with itself at that instant; collections of atoms form masses whose identity depends on membership of the same atoms (and changes when atoms are added/removed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of vegetables: continued organization/life defines plant identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant (oak) is the same plant as long as it partakes of the same continued life and organizational structure, even if material particles change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization that receives and distributes nourishment constitutes the vegetable life; new particles vitally united in the same organization do not destroy identity while the same life continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of animals: organization plus internal motion/life
rubrics_metrics.description: An animal is like an organized machine but differs because its motion (life) begins from within; animal identity is preserved by continued organization and internal life, not mere sameness of material particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a watch is organized parts fit for an end, but requires external force; an animal's life-motion comes from within, and continued organizational fitness preserves identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of man: same continued life in an organized body
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the same MAN consists in participation of the same continued life communicated to successively fleeting particles of matter in the same organized body; identity is not grounded solely in soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of 'soul-only' identity: if identity were only soul-based, the same soul united to different bodies across ages could make disparate historical persons identical, which is counterintuitive. The organized body's continued life is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of identity should match the idea the term denotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different names (SUBSTANCE, MAN, PERSON) stand for different ideas; the criterion of identity must correspond to the idea the name denotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misunderstandings about identity arise from failing to attend to the particular idea a term stands for; e.g., personal identity differs from substance identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity = consciousness-based identity
rubrics_metrics.description: PERSON denotes a thinking, intelligent being that can consider itself as the same thinking thing across times by virtue of consciousness; consciousness is inseparable from thinking and constitutes personal identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As far as consciousness can be extended backwards to past actions or thoughts, so far the identity of that person reaches. Consciousness (memory, reflection) unites past and present into one self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness continuity, not sameness of substance, grounds personal identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity depends on the continuity of consciousness rather than identity of immaterial substance or of material body; the same consciousness can persist despite changes of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: loss of limbs does not destroy personhood because the limbs lose the consciousness that made them part of self. Different substances that share the same consciousness can constitute one person; interruption of consciousness (forgetfulness, sleep) raises puzzles but does not change the criterion: identity extends as far as consciousness can be traced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity under change of thinking substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same thinking (immaterial) substance changing can preserve personal identity depends on whether consciousness of past actions can be transferred or represented to the new substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same consciousness can be represented to another thinking substance as one's own, then personal identity may be preserved; questions about transfer are metaphysical and, absent clearer knowledge of thinking substances, often deferred to theological considerations (goodness of God preventing wrongful transfers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Same immaterial substance may yield different persons if consciousness is lost
rubrics_metrics.description: The same immaterial substance continuing may constitute different persons if it loses all consciousness of its past existence and begins anew with no recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pre-existence theories where a soul existed in prior states without consciousness would make that pre-existent soul a different person than the one now conscious; numerical sameness of soul without continuity of consciousness does not preserve personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body as well as soul contributes to the making of a man (resurrection point)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person at resurrection may be the same despite a differently composed body, provided the same consciousness goes along with the soul inhabiting it; both body and soul play roles in making a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reconciles bodily difference with personal identity so long as consciousness continuity via the soul persists.
